header.title: Alexipharmaca: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Nicander of Colophon
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg0022.tlg002.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0022.tlg002.1st1K-gr: 'Palate' renders ὑπήνη, normally 'beard' or 'upper lip'. 'Hiccup' renders ἀλάλυξ, whose exact sense (hiccup, choking, retching) is uncertain. ἤλιθα (l. 25) may mean 'in abundance' rather than 'to no purpose'. The 'heart' and 'receiver' (ll. 21-22) are names for the upper opening of the stomach. Eubuleus is probably a title of Hades.
δέδηεν (l. 436) is taken as 'are held fast'; its sense is uncertain.
ῥάφανος (l. 527) is probably cabbage here, its older sense, rather than radish. ἀποφώλιος (l. 524), rendered 'baneful', can also mean 'empty, useless'.
537 λιπορρίνοιο is rare and its sense uncertain (‘sleek-skinned’, or perhaps ‘skin-shedding’); πανακηδέος (538), ‘grievous to all’, is also uncertain.

nodes.text: divided among themselves the richest farmland of the mainland,
seated beside the Clarian tripods of the Far-Shooter [Apollo]. —
But first, bitter and, for the mouth, hard to remedy,
learn of aconite, which the Acherusian banks
bring forth, where the chasm of Eubuleus, hard to escape from, [lies],
and the township of Priolas, overturned, has crashed down.
All the corners of the mouth, and the vaulted palate
and the gums, are puckered by its bitter drink; and about the upper
chest it coils, weighing down with an evil hiccup
the man suffering heartburn; and with anguish the top is gnawed,
the unclosed, upraised mouth of the lower belly,
which [some call] the 'heart' of the supper-vessel, while others
name it the 'receiver' of the gullet; and a gate leans on the first
beginnings of the guts, where all the food of mortals is carried in plenty;
and ever from the wet eyes a sweat trickles down;
and the belly, in turmoil, heaves up some winds to no purpose,
but many settle below, about the middle of the navel;
in the head there is a hateful heaviness, and under the temples a throbbing
comes thick and fast, and he sees double with his eyes,
like one overcome at night by neat wine.
And as when, having pressed the wild fruit of autumn,
onion shoots, mixed together; and the harm is warded off
by a well-cloved head of garlic, drunk fresh.
And you, when the tear of the poppy that carries its seed in a head
is drunk, may learn [the signs of] those sunk in sleep: for at the tips
of the limbs they grow cold, and the eyes do not open,
but stay just so, gleaming motionless beneath the eyelids;
and all about them, from distress, a strong-smelling sweat pours
in a flood; the face grows pale, the lips swell,
the bands of the jaw slacken, and a scant
cold breath, drawn from the throat, passes through;
you may give him to drink, the [scum] which the salt-maker always gathers
as it settles at the bottom, when he mixes waters with waters.
Let not the evil ferment of the earth harm a man,
often swelling up in the chest, at other times choking,
when it grows beneath the coils of a viper lurking deep in its lair,
drawing up its venom and the baneful breath of its jaws.
That evil ferment, which people call 'mushrooms'
generally, for each different kind has been given a different name.
But you should give either the curling head of cabbage,
or, clipping the [sprigs] that twist about the stem of rue,
thrusting in his hand, may he bring up the harmful bane.
But if [someone] is hurt by the hard-to-escape draught of the sleek-skinned
witch-lizard, grievous to all, which people call the salamander,
the one that not even the smoky flame of fire has harmed,
at once the depth of the tongue is inflamed, and in turn by numbing chill
they are overpowered, and a heavy, evil trembling loosens the limbs;
and staggering they crawl like an infant
on all fours; for their thinking wits are blunted;
and running thick over the flesh, livid on the surface,
weals spot [it], as the evil spreads.
